help.blurb: Decay (t60) time — how long the tail takes to fade out.
High-cut on the wet signal only — darkens the reverb without dulling the dry tone.
High-band decay relative to overall time; shorten it to model an absorptive room.
Size of the modeled space. Larger spaces are darker and grainier; very small values turn metallic.
Level of the early reflections (no effect on Spring types).
Level of the reverb tail.
Gap before the reverb starts; keeps a small space yet pushes the tail back from the dry signal.
Low-cut on the wet signal only — keeps the reverb from muddying the mix.
Modulation depth in the tail — thickens and lushes up the reverb, chorus-like.
Modulation rate of the tail movement.
Wet/dry blend. 0% = dry only, 100% = effect only.
Output level of the block.
Places the block output in the stereo field.
Input gain into the block.
Overdrives the spring-reverb circuit (Spring types).
Decay time of the low band — set independently for natural multi-band tails.
Crossover frequency splitting the low/high decay bands.
Ducker depth — how much the reverb dips while you play. 0 disables ducking.
Input level above which the ducker attenuates the reverb.
How the signal is routed when bypassed (e.g. muted, thru, or kept wet for trails).
Adds a global offset to this block’s Mix across all presets.
Echo density of the tail. Higher = smoother; lower lets individual repeats show.
HOLD sustains the current tail indefinitely; STACK holds it but keeps the input open to layer.
Selects which input(s) feed the block (left, right, sum, or stereo).
When on, this block ignores scene changes.
Removes the dry signal so only the wet effect is heard — useful in parallel/wet-only routings.
